title: Red Meat Abattoir Layout and Requirements

lessons.title: Principles of abattoir layout
lessons.html:
Why layout matters

A red meat abattoir must be designed so that meat moves from dirty to clean areas without ever going back, and so that people, equipment and waste do not cross-contaminate meat. Abattoirs must be registered and meet the structural and hygiene requirements under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations. The size and facilities required depend on the abattoir's category and throughput.

The forward flow principle

Animals and carcasses move in one direction: lairage → stunning and bleeding → dressing (hide removal, evisceration) → inspection → chilling → dispatch. Product never moves backwards to a dirtier area.

Dirty and clean areas

Dirty areasClean areas
Lairages and pensFinal dressing and inspection
Stunning and bleedingChillers
Hide removal (early stages)Cutting and deboning rooms
Gut and tripe roomDispatch area
Hide store, condemned material roomEdible offal room (after cleaning)

Physical separation (walls, distance) or separation by time keeps clean and dirty activities apart. Staff working in dirty areas should not walk into clean areas without changing protective clothing and washing.

Site requirements

  • Located away from sources of contamination such as refuse dumps, sewage works or industries producing smoke and dust.
  • Enough potable water supply and electricity.
  • All-weather roads and a fenced, secure site.
  • Effective wastewater and solid waste disposal.
  • Separate entrances for live animals and for dispatch of meat where possible.

lessons.title: Facilities and structural requirements
lessons.html:
What a red meat abattoir needs

Lairage

  • Pens with enough space, non-slip floors, drainage, shade and protection from weather.
  • Water available to all animals; feeding facilities if animals are held longer.
  • Isolation pen for sick or suspect animals.
  • Ante-mortem inspection area with good lighting.
  • Races designed for calm movement towards the stunning box.

Slaughter hall

  • Stunning box or restraining facility suited to the species.
  • Bleeding area with blood collection.
  • Overhead rail system so carcasses do not touch the floor or each other.
  • Inspection points with good lighting, hand-wash basins and knife sterilisers.
  • Detain rail or area for carcasses held for further inspection.
  • Separate rooms for gut processing, edible offal, heads and feet, hides and condemned material, as applicable.

Construction materials

  • Walls: smooth, impervious, light-coloured, easy to clean, to a required height.
  • Floors: impervious, non-slip, sloped to drains; drains with traps and grids.
  • Ceilings: smooth, cleanable, no flaking paint or condensation dripping onto meat.
  • Joints between walls and floors are rounded (coved) to prevent dirt build-up.
  • Doors and frames of non-corrosive material.
  • Lighting: adequate intensity, especially at inspection points, with protected light fittings.
  • Ventilation: removes steam, heat and odours; prevents condensation.

Chillers and dispatch

Chillers with capacity for the daily kill, rail spacing that allows air movement, thermometers or temperature recording, and a loading bay designed so vehicles can be loaded without exposing meat to contamination.

Staff facilities

Change rooms with separate clean and dirty sides, toilets that do not open directly into production areas, canteen, and hand-wash stations at entrances to production areas. Boot wash and footbath facilities.

Inspection facilities

An office for the meat inspection service, a lockable store for condemned material and equipment for sampling.

Key points

  • Product flows forward from dirty to clean areas and never back.
  • Separate clean and dirty areas physically or by time.
  • Surfaces must be smooth, impervious, light-coloured and easy to clean.
  • Lairages need water, shade, isolation pens and good races.
  • Inspection points need lighting, hand-wash basins and sterilisers.
